title: You're The Bottleneck
author: Patrick Dempsey
summary: Patrick Dempsey opens a new series on rethinking knowledge work in the AI era by arguing that his own career as an instructional designer was built on being a bottleneck. He traces the arc from teachers designing their own lessons, to professional instructional designers, to designers using AI, to teachers and then students using AI directly, and finally to AI systems that bypass even the student. The realization that changed everything for him is that expertise often earns its keep by making sure work cannot get done without the expert. He tests the usual comfort of subject matter expertise with a quick return on investment argument: if nonexpert AI output is somewhat worse but nearly free and instant, it often wins. His response was an anti-vision of removing himself from as many functions of his team's work as possible, and he reports that everything got better the less he had to do with it. The paradox he draws out is that making yourself less essential is how you stay relevant, and he previews a series on finding capacity, rethinking systems and building institutional intelligence.
points: Many careers rest on expertise functioning as a bottleneck, so AI exposes how much professional value came from being in the way rather than from the work itself.
Instructional design has moved step by step from the teacher to the designer to AI to the student, and each step removes a human gatekeeper.
Subject matter expertise is not a safe harbor, because nonexpert AI output that is cheaper and instant can beat a better output that depends on a salaried specialist.
Deliberately removing yourself from your team's workflows is a practical experiment, and the author found the work improved when he did.
The series ahead promises a playbook on finding capacity, rethinking systems, building institutional intelligence and redesigning work.
quotes: For me, the realization that changed everything is that I had essentially made my career on the basis of my “expertise” being a bottleneck to productivity.
AI makes it clear that no one necessarily needs me to do instructional design. But even before, if I had sufficiently enabled others to do the work I did, then they wouldn’t have needed me.
So I was a bottleneck. On purpose! My relevance was that I was in the way.

So, it seems to me that careers are built on people making themselves bottlenecks within systems such that if not for this person some aspect of the work can’t get done (or can’t get done to some standard).
Rather than making myself more valuable, I set out to remove myself as much as possible from all functions of our work to find out what would happen if I wasn’t in the way.
Here’s what I found: it totally worked. Everything got better the less I had to do with it. And that is the opportunity for knowledge work in the AI-era.
We’re moving from AI helping people do work to AI systems doing and coordinating the work themselves.
